summary: Hydrocortisone is the natural short-acting glucocorticoid identical to endogenous cortisol, with significant mineralocorticoid activity, making it the drug of choice for physiologic adrenal replacement (typically ~15-25 mg/day in divided doses). Oral tablets (5, 10, 20 mg) are also used for a wide range of inflammatory, allergic, rheumatic, dermatologic, hematologic and other conditions, with the initial dose ranging from 20 to 240 mg/day depending on severity. Dosing must be individualized, increased during physiologic stress (stress dosing), and tapered gradually rather than stopped abruptly to avoid adrenal crisis. Key concerns include infection masking and immunosuppression, hyperglycemia, fluid/sodium retention and hypokalemia, osteoporosis, and avoidance of live vaccines.
indications: Endocrine disorders: primary or secondary adrenocortical insufficiency (drug of first choice; add mineralocorticoid where needed), congenital adrenal hyperplasia, nonsuppurative thyroiditis, hypercalcemia of malignancy

Rheumatic disorders (short-term adjunct): rheumatoid arthritis (incl. juvenile), psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, acute gouty arthritis, bursitis, tenosynovitis, post-traumatic osteoarthritis, epicondylitis
Collagen diseases: systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic dermatomyositis (polymyositis), acute rheumatic carditis

Dermatologic diseases: pemphigus, bullous dermatitis herpetiformis, severe erythema multiforme (Stevens-Johnson), exfoliative dermatitis, mycosis fungoides, severe psoriasis, severe seborrheic dermatitis
Allergic states intractable to conventional treatment: severe allergic rhinitis, bronchial asthma, contact/atopic dermatitis, serum sickness, drug hypersensitivity reactions
Ophthalmic inflammatory/allergic processes: allergic conjunctivitis, keratitis, iritis/iridocyclitis, uveitis, optic neuritis, sympathetic ophthalmia
Respiratory diseases: symptomatic sarcoidosis, Loeffler's syndrome, berylliosis, fulminating/disseminated TB (with antituberculous therapy), aspiration pneumonitis
Hematologic disorders: idiopathic and secondary thrombocytopenic purpura in adults, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, erythroblastopenia, congenital hypoplastic anemia
Neoplastic diseases: palliative management of leukemias and lymphomas in adults and acute leukemia of childhood
Edematous states: to induce diuresis/remission of proteinuria in idiopathic or lupus nephrotic syndrome without uremia
Gastrointestinal diseases: ulcerative colitis and regional enteritis (critical periods)
Miscellaneous: tuberculous meningitis with subarachnoid block (with antituberculous therapy), trichinosis with neurologic or myocardial involvement

moa: Hydrocortisone is identical to endogenous cortisol; it diffuses across cell membranes and binds cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptors, and the complex modulates gene transcription to suppress inflammatory and immune mediators (cytokines, prostaglandins, leukotrienes), reduce capillary permeability, and stabilize leukocyte function. It also exerts mineralocorticoid activity at the renal tubule, promoting sodium and water retention and potassium excretion. At physiologic doses it replaces deficient endogenous corticosteroid; at higher doses it produces anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to hydrocortisone or any component
Administration of live or live-attenuated vaccines while on immunosuppressive doses
relative: Active or latent peptic ulcer disease
Nonspecific ulcerative colitis with risk of perforation, abscess, diverticulitis or fresh intestinal anastomoses
Ocular herpes simplex (risk of corneal perforation)
Known or suspected Strongyloides infestation; latent amebiasis
monitor: Bone mineral density on prolonged therapy

preg: Crosses the placenta; corticosteroids can cause fetal harm in animal studies (including cleft palate) and may suppress fetal/neonatal adrenal function. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk; physiologic replacement in maternal adrenal insufficiency is generally continued.
lact: Corticosteroids are excreted in human milk and could suppress growth or interfere with endogenous corticosteroid production in the nursing infant. Use with caution; physiologic replacement doses are generally considered compatible, but weigh benefit of breastfeeding against risk.
renal: Use with caution in renal insufficiency; no specific dose adjustment is stated in the label, but monitor fluid retention, blood pressure and electrolytes given mineralocorticoid activity.
hepatic: There is an enhanced effect of corticosteroids in patients with cirrhosis; use with caution and consider lower doses.

major: Live/live-attenuated vaccines: avoid during immunosuppressive doses (risk of disseminated infection, blunted response)
Hepatic enzyme inducers (phenobarbital, phenytoin, rifampin): increase corticosteroid clearance; may need higher hydrocortisone dose
moderate: CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, troleandomycin): decrease corticosteroid clearance; titrate dose to avoid steroid toxicity
Oral anticoagulants (warfarin): variable effect (enhanced or diminished); monitor coagulation indices
Potassium-depleting agents (loop/thiazide diuretics, amphotericin B): additive risk of hypokalemia
Antidiabetic agents (insulin, oral hypoglycemics): reduced glucose control; may need dose increases
minor: Chronic high-dose aspirin/salicylates: corticosteroids increase salicylate clearance (lower levels; risk of toxicity when steroid withdrawn); use caution in hypoprothrombinemia
interactions.food: Take with food to reduce GI irritation; high-sodium intake may worsen fluid retention
interactions.alcohol: Avoid or limit; additive risk of GI ulceration and bleeding
interactions.diagnostics: May suppress reactions to skin tests; can cause leukocytosis and alter electrolyte/glucose laboratory values

serious: Reactivation of tuberculosis, hepatitis B, or latent amebiasis/Strongyloides
Secondary adrenocortical and pituitary unresponsiveness (HPA suppression)
Osteoporosis with vertebral compression and long-bone fractures
Peptic ulcer with possible perforation and hemorrhage; pancreatitis
Posterior subcapsular cataracts, increased intraocular pressure, glaucoma
Congestive heart failure in susceptible patients
Steroid myopathy and muscle wasting; tendon rupture (esp. Achilles)
rare: Increased intracranial pressure with papilledema (pseudotumor cerebri), usually after treatment
emergency: Adrenal crisis from abrupt withdrawal or under-dosing during stress (hypotension, shock)

monitoring: Blood pressure and signs of fluid retention
Ocular exam (intraocular pressure, cataract) on prolonged use
Bone mineral density on long-term therapy
Adrenal function and disease flare during dose tapering
Screen for latent TB and hepatitis B before prolonged immunosuppressive therapy
counsel: Take with food, with the larger dose in the morning if divided
Never stop suddenly after prolonged use; the dose must be tapered
Carry a steroid alert card or medical ID
Increase dose and seek advice during illness, injury or surgery (stress dosing / sick-day rules)
Report fever or other signs of infection promptly; corticosteroids can mask infection
Avoid exposure to chickenpox and measles if not immune; report exposure
Avoid live vaccines while on therapy
Watch for and report mood changes, severe stomach pain or black stools, swelling, or increased thirst/urination
pk: Anti-inflammatory effect over hours; biologic effect within ~1-2 h
Plasma peak ~1 h after oral dose
Biologic effect ~8-12 h (short-acting; replacement needs divided dosing)
pearls: Drug of choice for adrenal replacement because it provides both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity
20 mg hydrocortisone ≈ 5 mg prednisone ≈ 4 mg methylprednisolone (approx. anti-inflammatory equivalence)
Short biologic half-life favors divided daily dosing to mimic the natural cortisol diurnal rhythm
Highest mineralocorticoid activity among the common glucocorticoids, so sodium/water retention and hypokalemia are prominent
Stress dosing is essential: increase dose during illness, trauma or surgery to prevent adrenal crisis
Drug-induced adrenal suppression can persist for months after stopping; treat any stress during that period as needing steroid cover
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip it and resume the regular schedule; do not double up. Patients on adrenal replacement should not skip doses and should contact their clinician if doses are missed during illness.
overdose: Acute overdose is rarely life-threatening. Chronic overdose produces hypercorticism/Cushingoid features, fluid and sodium retention, hypokalemia, hypertension and hyperglycemia. Management is supportive: monitor and correct electrolytes and glucose, manage blood pressure and fluid status, and taper the dose gradually rather than stopping abruptly.
